title: Paying Cash? You're Funding Someone's Credit Card Rewards
note: The sixth 3D short (2026-11-18, caaleb picked 'Card rewards scam' off a topic card after rejecting vanilla: a topic about the viewer's own money, with a villain). Every beat a counter close-up with the prop big in front of Data (data-3d-tabletop-beats). One number per beat, every claim in 'sources' with the source's own words.
lines: Every time you pay cash, you're paying for someone else's credit card rewards.
Stores pay a fee on every card swipe, so they quietly raise prices for everyone, even people paying cash.
A Federal Reserve study found the average cash-paying household hands about one hundred forty-nine dollars a year to card users.
And it flows uphill: the richest households collect about seven hundred fifty dollars a year, while the poorest pay in.
Your cash is quietly funding their points. So which do you use, cash or card?

sources.claim: Paying cash pays for card users' rewards
sources.says: On average, each cash-using household pays $149 to card-using households and each card-using household receives $1,133 from cash users every year.
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (Schuh, Shy, Stavins)

sources.claim: Stores pay a fee on card swipes and raise prices for everyone
sources.says: as card use becomes more frequent, merchants have raised their prices to compensate for card-processing charges
sources.publisher: HuffPost, on the Boston Fed study

sources.claim: About $149 a year from each cash-paying household to card users
sources.says: each cash-using household pays $149 to card-using households

sources.claim: The richest households collect about $750 a year; the poorest pay in
sources.says: after accounting for rewards paid to households by banks, the lowest-income household ($20,000 or less annually) pays $21 and the highest-income household ($150,000 or more annually) receives $750 every year

sources.claim: It flows from poorer to richer households
sources.says: the payment instrument transfer also induces a regressive transfer from low-income to high-income households

sets_why: the checkout where you pay cash, the stockroom where the store marks its prices up, a kitchen table at home where your savings go, a bank where the money ends up with the rich, back to the checkout to ask you
ideas: coins pour out of his hand and pile up under a giant gold credit card
he taps the card reader and every price tag on the boxes shoots up
he tips his piggy bank and its coins slide down a chute to a gold card
he pulls a lever and coins climb a ramp from a tiny shack to a mansion
he drops a gold card on a scale and it outweighs a whole stack of cash
storyboard: 1 hook (store): close at the checkout counter; a big gold credit card stands upright on a little stand at one end of the counter; Data holds his open hand over the counter and a stream of shiny coins pours out of it, rolling across to the card and piling up at its foot; he looks at us, annoyed.

2 swipe fee (warehouse): on a stockroom bench a row of three product boxes, each with a price tag on a stick; a card reader sits in front of Data; he taps the reader with one finger, it beeps green, and all three price tags shoot up higher on their sticks and turn red; he looks at us.

3 $149 (sorting_room): at the kitchen table a pink piggy bank sits at the top of a short tilted chute that runs down to a gold credit card lying flat; Data pushes the pig's back so it tips forward, coins pour out of its slot, slide down the chute and pile on the card; the pig is left empty.

4 uphill (bank): on a marble bank counter a tiny tin shack at the low end of a ramp and a big white model mansion on a riser at the top end; Data pulls a brass lever down and coins slide UP the ramp from the shack into a growing pile beside the mansion; he looks at us, unimpressed.

5 payoff (store): back at the checkout a brass balance scale; a fat stack of cash sits on the left pan; Data lays one gold credit card on the right pan and the card side drops hard, lifting the cash up; he looks at us and shrugs: cash or card?
